strengths: Mathematically sound use of topological covering maps to lift interval-valued quantities to cyclic groups, elegantly addressing the limitation of prior work (LCER)
Dramatic quantitative improvements in equivariance error: 4.66×10⁻⁶ for T³CEN vs 0.445 for LCER, with lifting error six orders of magnitude lower

Comprehensive experimental validation across synthetic datasets (3D Shapes, Small NORB), natural images (CIFAR, Caltech), and medical imaging (Camelyon17) with proper use of random seeds and error bars
Principled entropy-based approach to group order selection (Section 5.4, Figure 6) rather than arbitrary hyperparameter choices
Generalizability beyond HSL color space demonstrated through extensions to RGB shifts and scale transformations
Honest discussion of limitations including computational expense, parameter-capacity tradeoff, and degenerate lifting cases
weaknesses: Missing formal proof that HSL group convolution (Eq. 16) satisfies equivariance; paper only states 'it can be shown' without justification. Central claim needs rigorous support in main text

Degenerate lifting fundamentally limits information representation when input values equal kc/N, producing at most N/2+1 distinct values (Eq. 19). Impact on real-world performance when datasets contain these values is not characterized

Capacity-equivariance tradeoff inadequately addressed: Figure 8 shows accuracy degradation with increased orders (98.04% → lower), contradicting the benefit of perfect equivariance. While acknowledged, this deserves prominence as fundamental limitation

Limited practical improvements on standard benchmarks: Table 7 shows T³CEN performs worse than LCER on vanilla datasets; advantage exists primarily on synthetic color-shifted test sets. Real-world applicability unclear since most datasets lack artificial color shifts

No computational cost analysis provided despite acknowledging GCNNs are 'typically more computationally expensive'; missing runtime and FLOPs comparisons essential for practical adoption and ICML audience
Design choice of sinusoidal covering map π(θ) = (c/2)sin(θ) lacks justification; why this specific form? Other covering maps unexplored. Sensitivity analysis absent
Degenerate lifting presented as theoretical issue but treated heuristically; entropy-based order selection (H/N) is practical workaround not principled solution
Missing key baseline: no comparison with simple color augmentation during training, which could be simpler and more practical alternative
Dense notation with triple subscripts (gᵢⱼₖ, f₁₁₁) and tilded group actions (Eqs. 12-14) reduces clarity; modified group actions should use clearer notation

Real-world color imbalance (e.g., Camelyon17 non-uniform saturation variation in Figure 15) differs from synthetic uniform shifts; unclear how well method addresses naturally occurring color variations

strengths: Novel topological covering approach: Using covering maps to convert interval-valued quantities to cyclic groups is mathematically elegant and represents a genuine advance over prior approximate equivariance methods
Dramatic equivariance improvement: Equivariance error reduced 5+ orders of magnitude (4.66×10⁻⁶ vs 0.445) on saturation shifts compared to LCER
Rigorous mathematical framework: Clear presentation of group theory foundations with complete proofs of group axioms for all color channels
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple datasets (synthetic and real), thorough ablations, multiple random seeds, principled order selection via entropy analysis
Honest limitations discussion: Explicitly identifies when method fails (when color is signal) with quantified examples
Generalizability: Approach extends to RGB color space and geometric transformations like scale
weaknesses: Capacity-equivariance trade-off confounds results: Fixed parameter constraint requires reducing filter depth with higher lifting orders, making it difficult to isolate benefits of perfect vs. approximate equivariance from capacity effects; Appendix C.1 shows accuracy drops from 98.04% to 86.06% with increasing order

Modest real-world improvements: On vanilla datasets (Table 9), performance essentially matches LCER; Camelyon17 results are mixed with some configurations underperforming baselines; large gains primarily on synthetic datasets
Significant computational overhead: ~12x slower for full H4S4L4 configuration (1.59 vs 19.38 it/s) and 32GB vs 1GB memory, severely limiting practical applicability

Fundamentally limited applicability: Only effective when color varies between train/test AND varies independently of label; Section 5.5 shows 31.75% error vs 19.13% baseline when color is predictive (tomato ripeness)
Incomplete analysis of redundant representations: Lifting produces redundant outputs at specific values (~0.6-0.9% of pixels); impact on gradient flow and learning dynamics not analyzed
Questionable scale equivariance extension: Equation 24 applies modulo operations to pixel coordinates without properly implementing scale transformations

strengths: Novel theoretical contribution: Creative use of topological covering maps to endow interval-valued quantities with cyclic structure, enabling perfect (not approximate) equivariance to saturation and luminance shifts
Dramatic equivariance improvements: 6+ orders of magnitude reduction in equivariance error (4.66×10⁻⁶ vs 0.445) and lifting error (6.33×10⁻⁶ vs 8.65) compared to prior work
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Diverse datasets, multiple OOD settings, proper statistical reporting with multiple seeds, and rigorous mathematical foundation with formal proofs
Honest limitations discussion: Transparent characterization of failure modes (color-as-signal and no distribution shift) with quantitative analysis, demonstrating methodological maturity
Clear presentation and accessibility: Well-organized writing with effective visualizations (Figures 1-2) and proper mathematical exposition at multiple levels
Principled mathematical treatment: Rigorous group theory foundations with formal proofs of group properties, proper leveraging of established group convolution frameworks
weaknesses: Significant computational overhead inadequately addressed: 32× memory increase (32,842 MiB for H4S4L4) and 12× slowdown in training speed (1.59 it/s vs 19.38 it/s), with filter depth reduced to maintain parameter parity—this confounds architectural benefits with reduced capacity

Confounded experimental design: To keep parameters fixed, filter depth decreases with HSL order, making it impossible to isolate equivariance benefits from capacity penalties. Non-monotonic accuracy in Figure 9 suggests optimization is complex; equal-capacity comparisons needed

Modest practical improvements on real-world tasks: On vanilla datasets (Table 9), T³CEN often underperforms; on color-shifted datasets (Table 6), gains are inconsistent and marginal. Benefits mainly visible in medical imaging, a narrow domain

Unresolved redundant representations: Double-cover creates inherent redundancy at boundary values (Eq. 19), with only N/2+1 useful representations. Impact on learning dynamics unexplored despite 0.6-0.9% of pixels being affected

Group order selection remains heuristic: Entropy-based metric (Figure 6) requires dataset statistics and validation tuning, reducing principled nature. Optimal order is data-dependent with no closed-form solution
Limited justification for design choices: Why sine for π(θ)=(c/2)sin(θ)? Alternatives not discussed. Sensitivity to specific cover selection not analyzed

Incomplete secondary applications: RGB shift equivariance (Section 6) shown only qualitatively; scale equivariance mentioned but not thoroughly evaluated. These feel preliminary rather than integral contributions
Limited reproducibility: No code availability mentioned; lifting layer implementation details for handling redundancy sparse; some architectural modification choices under-documented
